contentBlocks.body: When you switch over the discriminant of a union, TypeScript removes each handled member as you go. After the last case, nothing is left, and the value's type is never: the type with no possible values. Passing it to a function that accepts only never turns that fact into a compile-time check.

Now add { kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number } to Shape. Without the default branch, area would silently return undefined for triangles. With it, the build fails at assertNever(shape) with Argument of type '{ kind: "triangle" ... }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never', pointing you at every switch that needs a new case.

Compile-time exhaustiveness does not protect you from data a newer server sends to an older client. Decide what the default branch does at runtime: throw (assertNever) for internal state, or return a safe fallback for data that crosses a network boundary.

knowledgeItems.prompt: In the default branch after handling every member of a union, what is the type of the switched value?

payload.explanation: Each case narrows the union; once all members are handled, no type remains, which TypeScript represents as never.

knowledgeItems.prompt: A teammate adds a new kind to the union but forgets one switch. What does assertNever(value) in the default branch cause?

choices: A compile error at that switch
The new kind is handled automatically
payload.answer: A compile error at that switch
payload.explanation: The unhandled member reaches the default branch, so value is no longer never, and passing it to a never parameter fails type checking.

payload.text: The type with no possible values, used for exhaustive checks, is called ____.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Describe each notification with an exhaustive switch over kind; unknown kinds from the server fall back to "Unsupported notification: <kind>".
